newsitem.title: USA: FOMC meeting -- What the Fed is looking at.
newsitem.headline: FOMC meeting -- What the Fed is looking at.

text.p: The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) is meeting on Tuesday to discuss the appropriate level of the federal funds rate with an economy marked by above-trend growth, tight labor markets, healthy consumer spending and moderate inflation.

In three separate testimonies between late January and mid-March, Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan put financial markets on notice that Fed policy must remain preemptive since "it is not the conditions that prevail today that are critical but rather those likely to prevail six to 12 months from now."
-- Fed sources told Reuters the Fed looks at the longer trend, six-quarter average of the Gross Domestic Product.
-- The six-quarter GDP average for the period ended in mid-1995 stood at 2.5 percent. Coupled with rising inventories, it was a sharp deceleration from 3.5 percent at yearend 1994. The Fed eased.
-- The six-quarter GDP average fell further to 2.0 percent at yearend 1995. The Fed eased at two consecutive meetings.
-- The six-quarter GDP average bounced back to 2.3 percent in mid-1996 and was accompanied by a drop in the unemployment rate to 5.5 percent. The Fed put a tightening bias in place.

-- Employment Cost Index was up 3.0 percent year-over-year by yearend 1996 but its wages component rose faster, up 3.3 percent. The labor benefits component is believed to have bottomed out, pointing to higher overall labor costs in 1997.

-- The measurement of productivity remains imprecise and may be understated. Some economists say this would allow for sustainable, non-inflationary growth to be around 2.5 percent rather than 2.0 percent, as previously estimated.
-- The Fed lacks a public constituency for an aggressive anti-inflation stance in an already low inflation environment.

March 20, testimony before the Joint Economic Committee: "We stressed the importance of acting promptly -- ideally preemptively -- to keep inflation low over the intermediate term and to promote price stability over time."

-- February 26, Humphrey-Hawkins testimony: "The FOMC continues to see the distribution of inflation risks skewed to the upside... The relative modest gains we have experienced are a temporary rather than a lasting phenomenon."
-- "To be sure, 1997 is not 1994. In February 1997, our concern is a matter of relative risks rather than of expected outcomes."
-- MEASUREMENT PROBLEMS AND IMPACT FOR POLICY:

-- January 21, Senate Budget Committee: "The evidence that inflation has been slower and that real growth has been faster than the official measures indicate, has been welcome... Because such a revision implies faster growth in potential output as well as actual ouput, it does not alter the relationship between resource utilization and inflation."x
-- At yearend 1996, the six-quarter GDP average had climbed back to 2.8 percent. The first-quarter 1997 GDP is likely to come out above trend as well, analysts said.
-- Some analysts pointed out that, since monetary policy operates with a six-month lag, the current pickup in economic activity may stem from the lack of Fed action in mid-1996.
-- Consumer spending remained healthy through the sixth year of the expansion, with retail sales up a 5.1 percent year-over-year, matching the nominal GDP growth rate.
-- Year-over-year core Consumer Price Index seemed to have bottomed out at around 2.5 percent since the fall of 1996.
Fed watchers expect the Fed to hike the 5.25-percent funds rate on Tuesday for the first hike since February 1, 1995.
In a March 20 Reuters survey of U.S. primary dealers:
-- 18 expected a 25-basis-point hike on March 25, no move at the following FOMC meeting on May 20.
-- 10 expected a 25-point hike on March 25 and May 20.
-- 1 saw a 25-point hike "maybe" on March 25 or May 20
-- 3 did not expect a move on either March 25 or May 20.
-- (*) indicates the firm changed its forecast or altered it to clarify the date:
